To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Cd59a(-/−) mice, deficient for a complement regulator, develop an increased age-related complement system activation in the RPE/choroid, that does not result in retinal degeneration, but is sufficient to induce a subretinal macroglial response.
Cd59a deficiency leads to a dysregulation of complement in the RPE with age, which is not sufficient to induce retinal degeneration or retinal dysfunction.
Cd59a deficiency in the retina leads to an age-dependent dysregulation of complement activation in the RPE and choroid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular changes that occur in the retina and choroid during normal aging and how these processes are affected by the presence or absence of the complement regulator Cd59a.
the molecular and cellular basis of age-related retinal degeneration.
the pathogenesis and treatment of AMD, the leading cause of blindness in the Western world.
